newsitem.title: UK: Oil near six-year highs on pre-winter shortages.
newsitem.headline: Oil near six-year highs on pre-winter shortages.

text.p: Buoyant world oil prices opened near six-year highs on Tuesday after resuming on Monday the storming bull run which has pushed crude values up 40 percent in the last four months.
London futures for international benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude traded down three cents a barrel at $24.83 after adding 88 cents on Monday to set a new post-Gulf War high.

Brent has shot up $7 a barrel since mid-June, hitting a $24.92 peak on Monday, driven by concerns over tensions in the oil-rich Middle East and persistently low stocks of heating oil in western markets.
With the exception of the 1990-1991 Gulf crisis, crude has not been as costly since the second oil price shock in the wake of the 1979 Iranian revolution.

Fresh fighting between rival Kurdish factions in Iraq since the weekend has served to remind markets of the missing crude supplies previously expected under a United Nations oil-for-food exchange with Iraq.

"Iraqi oil exports under U.N. resolution 986 this year are now impossibly remote, and in the light of recent developments in the Kurdish areas of Iraq, they may well not begin until the second half of 1997 -- if at all," said the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES) in London.

The U.N. deal, signed in May and worth several hundred thousand barrels per day of crude supplies, was suspended at the end of August after Baghdad sent troops to intervene on behalf of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) against its rival, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK). The KDP on Tuesday launched a counter-attack after the PUK regained on Sunday the region's largest city, Sulaimaniya.
The KDP accused Iran of sending troops and arms to lead PUK attacks over the weekend, but Tehran denied any involvement.

The renewed fighting underlined how difficult it would be for the United Nations to guarantee the safety of aid distribution monitors in northern Iraq under the oil-for-food exchange any time soon, said CGES chief economist Leo Drollas.

"Oil sales from Iraq are almost certainly out of the question now for some time to come. The oil market looks set to remain tight through the coming winter," he added. Dealers said low stocks of heating oil in the United States and Europe in the approach to winter had also pushed futures markets higher as refinery buyers and traders hedged against rising supply costs.
The fund managers that control huge investment accounts have also joined the oil rally in force.
Heating oil stocks are running about 10 percent down on last year's already slim levels in both northwest Europe and the United States.
Analysts say oil companies are partly to blame. Keen to cut costs by maintaining low inventories, some refiners have been caught short in the scramble to replenish winter stocks.
A refinery fire in Toledo, Ohio on Monday underlined how sensitive oil prices are likely to be this winter to supply outages, traders said.
"This is a very jumpy market -- any supply disruptions are likely to have a disproportionate effect," said a London-based oil trader.
Meanwhile oil markets look unlikely to get any help from extra OPEC supplies.
The oil cartel led by Saudi Arabia has no plans to raise output for fear of rocking the boat and undermining a market which is providing windfall extra revenues, Gulf sources said last week.
